item.problem_title: A hazard ratio is reported where the estimand was a weighted per-protocol effect among the grace-period compatible
item.problem_statement: Hazard ratios, odds ratios and model coefficients are routinely presented without naming the intervention, the population, the time horizon or the strategy for each intercurrent event. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement both require that objectives, estimands and sensitivity analyses be aligned, and applied reporting has not caught up. A correctly executed clone-censor-weight analysis with a grace period estimates a marginal contrast between prespecified strategies in the baseline eligible population, and where the artificial censoring enforces adherence that contrast is per-protocol. A bare hazard ratio discloses none of this: not the intervention, not the strategies, not the population, not the horizon, not the handling of intercurrent events. It is therefore read as an intention-to-treat contrast by default, and nothing in the presentation contradicts that reading.

item.problem_title: The visit process is treated as a nuisance to be imputed rather than as part of the causal structure
item.problem_statement: Biomarkers and diagnoses are observed when a patient attends care and a clinician orders a test. That visit process depends on latent severity, on prior treatment and often on an impending outcome, so missing-at-random conditional on the recorded history can fail precisely because the recording is itself informative, last observation carried forward constructs a history in which the absence of measurement was itself evidence, and conditioning on having been observed can induce selection bias. Three estimator families now address this: multiply robust estimation under covariate-driven observation times, calibrated inverse probability weights under irregular visits, and continuous-time weights built from a marked point process. item.problem_statement: An internally valid estimate need not apply to the health system, population or calendar period where the decision will be made. Transporting an observational contrast requires treatment exchangeability in the source, effect exchangeability across samples conditional on a sufficient measured set, and positivity for both treatment and sampling. item.problem_title: Subgroup effects are estimated where overlap is worst, and the groups with worst overlap are often the protected ones
item.problem_statement: Causal forests and meta-learners estimate heterogeneous treatment effects and inherit every identification assumption of the base analysis without relaxing any of them. A subgroup analysis therefore requires subgroup-specific assessment of exchangeability, measurement validity, positivity and uncertainty, and apparent heterogeneity can reflect differential measurement or differential access rather than differential biology. Two further requirements are routinely skipped. Adaptively chosen subgroups need selection-aware inference, because the reported interval otherwise conditions on a subgroup the data chose. And restricting to regions with adequate overlap changes the target population rather than fixing the estimate, so it has to be reported as a change of question. It provides no evidence on inference for weighted sustained-treatment estimators, rare competing events, or reporting effective sample size.

item.problem_title: Large databases yield small effective samples after eligibility, comparator restriction and weighting
item.problem_statement: A database of millions can carry very little information about a specific target trial once strict eligibility, active-comparator restriction and weighting have been applied, and extreme weights reduce the effective sample size far below the nominal count. Conventional asymptotic inference then becomes unreliable, most sharply for rare competing events and for subgroup effects, which are the quantities decision makers ask about. Papers continue to report the nominal number of patients, which for a weighted longitudinal analysis is not the quantity that governs the variance, and no convention requires the effective size to appear beside it.

item.problem_title: Code, phenotype logic, weight diagnostics and rejected protocol versions are not available for emulations
item.problem_statement: The TARGET statement asks for the target protocol, its data mapping, the estimands, the assumptions, the estimates and the sensitivity analyses, and is a transparency instrument rather than a risk-of-bias certification. An emulation is not externally auditable when its final analysis code, its complete versioned phenotype logic and its weight diagnostics are unavailable, and in current practice they are: most emulations are irreproducible in operative detail despite faithful protocol reporting. Where the real data cannot be shared, code plus a documented schema, a container and synthetic fixtures establishes that the pipeline executes and what it does; it does not reproduce the published estimate, and auditability rather than reproduction is what such a release can deliver. Material protocol amendments belong in a versioned decision log, which nothing currently requires.

item.problem_title: There is no assumption dashboard, so diagnosable and undiagnosable assumptions are reported alike
item.problem_statement: Exchangeability and consistency cannot be established from observed data. Neither, strictly, can positivity, model correctness or phenotype validity: the available checks reveal or falsify particular problems and certify none of them. Current reports blur both distinctions. A propensity-score overlap plot is offered and the reader infers that the assumptions have been checked, when the plot is a partial diagnostic of one of them and silent on the rest. No standard panel exists, so what appears varies by author and by journal, and an absent diagnostic cannot be distinguished from one that was run and not reported. A single panel cannot be adequate for every design, which is a constraint on the solution rather than an argument against it.
item.evidence: Three concrete checks are named for one assumption that the registry treats as undiagnosable in practice, model correctness: refit under different specifications, refit under different orderings of the confounder density factorization, and compare the estimate against a nonparametric natural-course estimate. They are offered as informal diagnostics with no threshold and no reporting convention, so they narrow the entry rather than close it.
